themes.theme: Regulatory sandboxes: establishment, deadlines and resourcing
themes.definition: Duties and powers to set up and resource AI regulatory sandboxes, the supervised environments in which AI is developed and tested before it reaches the market or a service.
themes.what_is_set_out: The AI Act requires each Member State to ensure that its competent authorities establish 'at least one AI regulatory sandbox at national level, which shall be operational by 2 August 2026' (Art. 57(1); Recital 138), and the Digital Omnibus moves the date to 2 August 2027. Member States must ensure that authorities 'allocate sufficient resources' (Art. 57(4)), and Recital 138 asks for 'the adequate resources for their functioning, including financial and human resources'; the Commission 'may provide technical support, advice and tools', and authorities may ask the AI Office and the Board for support and guidance (Art. 57(1), 57(15)). The only sandbox aimed at public bodies is a power, not a duty: the European Data Protection Supervisor 'may' set one up for EU institutions, bodies, offices and agencies (Art. 57(3), kept by the Omnibus); the Omnibus adds a power for the AI Office to run a Union-level sandbox for Art. 75(1) systems with priority access for SMEs and SMCs. The 2022 JRC handbook had already recommended reinforcing sandboxes across the EU, and EU043 mentions sandbox testing and real-world testing as routes the Act provides. No passage reserves places or money in national sandboxes for tools used by public bodies.
themes.holders: Member States and their national competent authorities ('establishing authorities'); the Commission; the AI Office and the Board; the European Data Protection Supervisor; under the Omnibus, the AI Office for a Union-level sandbox.
themes.binding: Statutory duty on Member States with a fixed date ('shall ensure', 'shall be operational by'); no consequence for missing it is stated. The Commission, EDPS and AI Office roles are powers ('may'). Recitals, the EU043 mention and the JRC handbook are non-binding.
themes.checks: n/a here; the testing that sandboxes host is described in the next theme.

themes.theme: What sandboxes and real-world testing give participants
themes.definition: The supervision, guidance, reports, tools, access and data permissions that sandboxes and real-world testing offer to those who take part.
themes.what_is_set_out: Within a sandbox, competent authorities 'shall provide, as appropriate, guidance, supervision and support' on identifying risks to fundamental rights, health and safety, on testing and on mitigation (Art. 57(6)), and at the end 'an exit report detailing the activities carried out in the sandbox and the related results and learning outcomes' (Art. 57(7)), which, per coder note, providers may use to show compliance in conformity assessment or market surveillance. Access is free for SMEs apart from exceptional costs, SMEs get priority access, sandbox learning is to help with conformity assessment, and participants are directed to pre-deployment services such as guidance, standardisation help and testing facilities (Arts 58(2)(d)-(e), 62(1)(a), 58(3)). Sandboxes are to 'facilitate the development of tools and infrastructure for testing, benchmarking, assessing and explaining' accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity (Art. 58(2)(i)), and carry the legal basis to reuse personal data for public-interest AI, including AI developed by a public authority (Art. 59(1); Recital 140). The Digital Omnibus adds access to 'physical public infrastructure' for real-world testing of certain AI-enabled products (Art. 60a(4)). The resources are framed for providers and prospective providers; deployers, and public bodies as buyers, are not named as recipients.
themes.holders: National competent authorities running sandboxes (guidance, supervision, exit reports, cost recovery); Member States (priority access for SMEs; access to public infrastructure under the Omnibus); providers and prospective providers, including public authorities developing public-interest AI, as recipients. Several provisions are passive and name no holder.
themes.binding: Mostly statutory ('shall provide', 'shall be directed'), softened by 'as appropriate' and 'where relevant'; the data permission applies only when every listed condition is met. No consequence is stated if authorities fall short.
themes.checks: Trigger: before placing on the market or putting into service, during the sandbox or the real-world test. Compared against: the Regulation's requirements and identified risks [inference]; the dimensions named are accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity. Metric or threshold: not stated. Who: the provider tests, under the supervision of the competent authority. What happens with the result: recorded in an exit report that may be used in conformity assessment or market surveillance (coder note).

themes.theme: Testing facilities, innovation hubs and technical support structures
themes.definition: Shared EU and national facilities and support structures that offer testing, experimentation and technical or scientific advice.
themes.what_is_set_out: The AI Act creates 'Union AI testing support structures' that 'shall also provide independent technical or scientific advice' when the Board, the Commission or market surveillance authorities ask (Art. 84(2)); the coder note records that who these structures are is not stated. Recital 145 says the AI-on-demand platform, the European Digital Innovation Hubs (EDIHs) and testing and experimentation facilities (TEFs) 'should contribute to the implementation of this Regulation', mainly through technical and scientific support to providers and notified bodies; deployers are not named. The two JRC reports present the same facilities as help for public administrations: the 2022 handbook says EDIHs 'could' offer experimentation facilities, training and an environment for sandboxing, with support aimed at the public sector, and that TEFs offer testing of 'mature technology' in real or close-to-real conditions; the 2025 report says EDIHs 'provide technical support and experimentation facilities to help in efforts towards AI adoption', with a reinforced public-sector focus (coder note). The AI Act points these facilities at compliance; the JRC reports point them at adoption.
themes.holders: Union AI testing support structures (designated by the Commission); the AI-on-demand platform, EDIHs and TEFs (established by the Commission and Member States); the Commission (facilitates access to TEFs for accredited bodies).
themes.binding: Art. 84(2) is a statutory task ('shall'), triggered only on request; Recitals 145 and 147 use 'should' and 'to the extent possible'; the JRC texts describe or suggest ('could', 'can').
themes.checks: Trigger: on request (Art. 84) or during development and experimentation. Compared against: not stated. Metric or threshold: not stated. Who: the support structures, EDIHs and TEFs. What happens with the result: advice goes to the Board, Commission or market surveillance authority that asked; otherwise not stated.

quotes.quote: Union AI testing support structures shall also provide independent technical or scientific advice at the request of the Board, the Commission, or of market surveillance authorities.

Experimentation activities can draw on resources of Testing and Experimentation Facilities (TEFs), which are technology infrastructures with specific expertise and experience in testing mature technology
For instance, the EDIHs provide technical support and experimentation facilities to help in efforts towards AI adoption.

themes.theme: Independent and outside experts for evaluation and testing
themes.definition: Independent experts and outside services that authorities or operators may bring in to evaluate or test AI.
themes.what_is_set_out: For general-purpose models, the Commission 'may decide to appoint independent experts to carry out evaluations on its behalf', including from the scientific panel, whose members must meet independence criteria (Art. 92(2); Recital 164 for the AI Office). Union testing support structures give 'independent technical or scientific advice' on request (Art. 84(2)). Recital 67 mentions that data governance requirements 'can be complied with' by using third parties offering certified compliance services, including verification of data set integrity and of training, validation and testing practices, without naming any. The Commission's prohibited-practices guidelines suggest, as a possible safeguard, 'prior written and motivated expert opinion relating to t he specific use case', which the deployer would obtain (EU043), and EU121 lets signatories 'involve independent experts' to red-team their marking and detection solutions or test them under supervision in a sandbox. In every passage outside expertise is optional: a power, a mention or a suggestion.
themes.holders: The Commission and the AI Office (appoint experts); the scientific panel; Union AI testing support structures; unnamed third-party compliance services; deployers (obtain expert opinion, EU043); EU121 signatories that provide generative AI systems.
themes.binding: Powers and options only: 'may decide', 'should be able to', 'can be complied with', 'could include', 'may involve'. No passage requires outside review.
themes.checks: Trigger: the Commission's decision to evaluate a general-purpose model; a request (Art. 84); or the operator's choice. Compared against: not stated, except robustness to adversarial attacks (EU121). Metric or threshold: not stated. Who: independent experts, the scientific panel, certified third parties. What happens with the result: evaluations are carried out on the Commission's behalf; nothing further is stated.

quotes.quote: The Commission may decide to appoint independent experts to carry out evaluations on its behalf, including from the scientific panel established pursuant to Article 68.
Such safeguards could include, for example, prior written and motivated expert opinion relating to t he specific use case.

Signatories may involve independent experts in the testing of their solutions, especially to evaluate robustness to adversarial attacks through red teaming and/or conduct such testing and evaluation under regulatory supervision in the context of AI regulatory sandboxes

The requirements related to data governance can be complied with by having recourse to third parties that offer certified compliance services including verification of data governance, data set integrity, and data training, validation and testing practices

themes.theme: Commission guidelines and pointers to interpretive sources
themes.definition: Official guidance issued or promised by the Commission and the AI Office to explain how to apply the AI Act, and the other sources those guidelines point readers to.
themes.what_is_set_out: The AI Act requires the Commission to 'develop guidelines on the practical implementation of this Regulation', covering the high-risk requirements, value-chain duties, prohibitions, substantial modification and transparency, and to pay particular attention to SMEs, 'local public authorities' and the sectors most affected (Art. 96(1)). The Digital Omnibus extends the guidelines to deployers' obligations under Art. 26, requires the Board to be involved, adds SMCs and a new topic to be published by 1 August 2027 (coder note), and its Recital 40 says support measures for the high-risk rules should be 'in place in due time'. Two guidelines in the set describe themselves as this resource: EU043 on prohibited practices and the Article 50 guidelines both say they 'serve as practical guidance' to competent authorities, providers and deployers. They in turn point to EDPB guidelines on profiling, to EU consumer law as 'a valid source of inspiration', to the Commission's guidelines on the definition of an AI system, and to joint Commission-EDPB guidance that is still 'under preparation'. The guidelines for general-purpose AI (EU088) supply concrete methods for estimating training compute, hardware-based or architecture-based, with worked examples, and say the AI Office 'is dedicated to supporting providers' to comply by 2 August 2027 without saying how.
themes.holders: The Commission (with the Board under the Omnibus); the AI Office (support to general-purpose model providers); the EDPB (profiling guidelines) and the Commission with the EDPB jointly (forthcoming).
themes.binding: The duty to issue guidelines is statutory ('shall develop'), with no consequence stated; the guidelines themselves are interpretive and non-binding [inference]. The pointers are mentions only.
themes.checks: Mostly n/a. The EU088 compute-estimation methods measure a model (how much computation went into training), not its outputs: trigger not stated; compared against a threshold not stated in these passages; who: providers; what happens with the result: not stated.

themes.theme: Help channels, information platforms, templates and awareness campaigns
themes.definition: Channels, platforms, standard templates and campaigns through which authorities answer questions and spread information about the AI Act to operators.
themes.what_is_set_out: Member States 'shall' organise awareness-raising and training on the Regulation tailored to SMEs, deployers and, 'as appropriate, local public authorities', and use or create channels 'to provide advice and respond to queries' (Art. 62(1)(b)-(c); Recital 143). The AI Office 'shall' provide standardised templates as specified by the Board, a 'single information platform' for all operators, and communication campaigns on the Regulation's obligations (Art. 62(3)); Recital 143 assigns the templates and the platform to the Commission. National competent authorities 'may provide guidance and advice', in particular to SMEs, taking account of the Board's and the Commission's guidance (Art. 70(8)); the Digital Omnibus keeps this and adds SMCs. Local public authorities are the only public bodies named as recipients, and only 'as appropriate'; what the templates and advice contain is left open.
themes.holders: Member States; the AI Office and the Commission; national competent authorities; the Board (specifies templates on request).
themes.binding: Statutory duties on Member States and the AI Office ('shall'); a power for national competent authorities ('may'); recital wording 'should'. No consequence is stated.

themes.theme: Standards, codes of practice and codes of conduct
themes.definition: Standards, codes of practice and voluntary codes of conduct offered as ways to meet, or go beyond, the rules.
themes.what_is_set_out: Recital 121 gives standardisation 'a key role to provide technical solutions to providers to ensure compliance', and the coder note adds that harmonised standards are a means to demonstrate conformity; the passage does not name the standards bodies. For general-purpose models the AI Office 'shall encourage and facilitate' Union-level codes of practice (Art. 56(1)), which EU088 says 'lay down specific measures' that model providers 'may implement' to comply. The Digital Omnibus adds a Commission duty to 'encourage and facilitate' codes of practice on detecting, marking and labelling AI-generated content (Art. 50(7)), and asks the AI Office and Member States to account for the needs of SMEs and SMCs when facilitating voluntary codes of conduct (Art. 95(4)). EU043 only notes that minimal-risk systems may follow voluntary codes and that 'professional due diligence practices and industry standards' can help prevent harm, without naming any. In every passage the resource is a facilitated process or a general reference, not a published standard.
themes.holders: Standardisation bodies (not named in the passage); the AI Office and the Board; the Commission; Member States; providers and deployers who choose to adopt codes.
themes.binding: Facilitation duties on EU bodies ('shall encourage and facilitate', 'shall take into account'); adherence by operators is voluntary ('may implement', 'may voluntarily adhere'); the recital uses 'should'.

themes.theme: Marking, detection and labelling tools for AI-generated content
themes.definition: Tools for marking, detecting and labelling AI-generated or manipulated content and for identifying AI agents, and who must make them available to whom.
themes.what_is_set_out: The Article 50 guidelines say that the provider of a system generating synthetic content 'is obliged to ensure that the means of detection are available to the persons potentially exposed to the content' and, per coder note, to authorities and researchers; providers may rely on a marking solution from an upstream model provider or a third party, and deployers of deep fakes may use labelling tools offered by very large platforms and search engines, in both cases without losing their own responsibility. The guidelines recommend standardised disclosure practices and labels 'Where available and appropriate', which implies such labels may not yet exist, and point to EU Digital Identity Wallets as a means to identify AI agents. EU121, a code of practice for signatories under Article 50, is more specific: signatories 'will make available a detection solution' to deployers, users, integrators, exposed end-users and other legitimate parties, 'will always provide free access to their detection solution, without any restriction on the volume of requests' to market surveillance authorities, regulators, law enforcement, media and researchers, and will hand a discontinued solution to market surveillance authorities; model-level watermarking and documentation for deployers are only encouraged, and independent red-teaming is optional. The Digital Omnibus asks the Commission to facilitate codes of practice on detection, marking and labelling. [inference] These tools matter to public bodies both as deployers that publish AI-generated material and as authorities that need to verify content.
themes.holders: Providers of generative AI systems (detection means, marking); upstream model providers and third parties (marking solutions); providers of very large online platforms and search engines (labelling tools); EU121 signatories; the Commission (codes of practice).
themes.binding: The detection duty rests on Art. 50(2), with fines (the 'if not met' field cites para 152); reliance on others' tools is permissive and 'without prejudice' to the operator's own responsibility (coder notes). EU121 commitments bind only signatories who choose to adhere, monitored by market surveillance authorities with no stated consequence; several measures are 'encouraged' or optional ('may').
themes.checks: Trigger: whenever content is encountered and a check is requested (EU121: free access 'without any restriction on the volume of requests'). Compared against: the marking embedded by the provider (watermarks or other marks). Metric or threshold: not stated; no detection accuracy or error rate is given. Who: deployers, exposed persons, market surveillance and other authorities, researchers. What happens with the result: not stated in these passages.

themes.theme: Guidance and templates from data protection and cybersecurity authorities
themes.definition: Guidance, templates and reading lists from data protection and cybersecurity authorities that help organisations manage the risks of AI.
themes.what_is_set_out: The EDPS orientations describe themselves as 'practical advice' to EU institutions on processing personal data when using generative AI (version 2, revised in light of EDPS monitoring, per coder note); they offer an EDPS template for deciding whether a data protection impact assessment is needed, point to the EDPS risk guidance, to a CNIL sheet on web-scraping safeguards, and to a reading list that includes the OECD catalogue of tools and metrics. The EDPS risk guidance says it complements the EDPS toolkit on impact assessments and prior consultation and the generative AI orientations. The EDPB (EU074) gives supervisory authorities 'a non -prescriptive and non -exhaustive list' of elements for assessing a claim that an AI model is anonymous, including, per coder note, model testing and resistance to attacks, plus examples of mitigating measures and a pointer to its legitimate-interest guidelines. ENISA's note offers 'an initial set of recommendations' on capabilities against AI-enabled cyber threats, described as not an all-inclusive checklist (coder note), and points to its NIS2 implementation guidance. All of it is non-binding, and the EDPS material is addressed to EU institutions rather than national public bodies.
themes.holders: The EDPS; the EDPB; ENISA; CNIL and other bodies named in reading lists (mentions only).
themes.binding: Non-binding guidance; the EDPB list is expressly non-prescriptive; ENISA's recommendations are 'neither exhaustive nor mutually exclusive' (coder note). No consequence is stated.
themes.checks: Anonymity of AI models (EU074): trigger: when a supervisory authority assesses a controller's claim; compared against: a list of possible elements including model design, analysis, testing and resistance to attacks (coder note); metric or threshold: not stated; who: supervisory authorities; what happens with the result: not stated here. DPIA template (EDPS): used to decide whether an impact assessment is needed [inference: before processing]. Otherwise n/a.

themes.theme: Pointers to technical tools for explainability, bias, privacy and vulnerability checks
themes.definition: Technical tools, mostly from third parties, that documents name for explaining outputs, auditing bias, protecting privacy or triaging vulnerabilities.
themes.what_is_set_out: The EDPS risk guidance names, as possible measures, explainability techniques 'such as LIME or SHAP', the IBM AI Fairness 360 and Aequitas toolkits for bias audits of training data, of the system and of analysts' interpretation of outputs (coder note), a framework for the privacy-utility trade-off in synthetic data, and MemHunter to detect memorisation of personal data by large language models. It also points to its own TechDispatch on explainable AI and to guidance from the UK Information Commissioner's Office on explaining results, a UK source cited in an EU document. ENISA points to the Exploit Prediction Scoring System and the Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange to help organisations prioritise vulnerabilities; the coder note records that these are not AI tools. Every passage is a mention or footnote rather than an official offer, and none says how to use the tool, what result is acceptable, or who in a public body should run it.
themes.holders: Tool developers (academic authors, IBM, FIRST, spring-epfl contributors, the ICO); the EDPS and ENISA point to them; users are not named (nearest: EU institutions as controllers).
themes.binding: Mentions only ('it is possible to use', 'Consideration of', 'could be implemented'); no obligation.
themes.checks: Trigger: not stated. Compared against: not stated (the fairness and explainability criteria inside the tools are not described). Metric or threshold: not stated. Who: not stated. What happens with the result: not stated.
